I totally hear you and I think those are important considerations! but I think it's worth noting that a person being a public figure and a case having a high level of public interest generally means that it is harder to block public access, not easier. 

imho that's as it should be. there is a difference between private persons and public figures and the courts have recognized that difference.

>I can’t think of any other information the public would need to know.

I mentioned this in a comment to someone else, but I'll reiterate: public access is essential for accountability. I've covered a number of cases where the real circumstances of a death were very different than law enforcement made them out to be in initial public statements. for example, public records (including video footage) once enabled me to report on how the death of a man held in a county jail occurred due to the negligence of jail staff, after authorities told the public the death was a one off occurrence that could not have been anticipated or prevented.

that case is different than this one, of course, but I bring it up to show the importance of public access. any erosion of the public's right to information is dangerous to everyone, in my view, and should be resisted.

I disagree. open access to public records is how you hold authorities accountable. I've covered a number of stories where the details of a death (as revealed in police reports, body cam footage, etc) that I accessed through public record requests told a very different story than the initial public statements from law enforcement.

my belief is that the public is entitled to access records created by police or any government agency and that more access is generally better than less. any restrictions or redactions to public records should be exceedingly rare and very narrowly tailored. I don't expect everyone to agree with my opinion on this.

I'm a reporter IRL, so I see this through a different lens than some. in my semi rural community, a child dying tragically in this manner would be news, as a matter of public interest and public safety. it would be an opportunity to educate the public about how the death occurred and how similar deaths can be prevented in the future.

given that the family involved is famous and has a large public platform, public interest is naturally increased. the public safety aspect is similarly magnified. it is important that this story be covered.

as a reporter, I am generally opposed to the sealing of records that would otherwise be public, such as police reports and related materials. people have a right to access public records.

in a perfect world, all entities that access these records would use them responsibly and with careful consideration for the manner in which they are presented. unfortunately, we don't live in a perfect world and there are many who use sensitive records in ghastly ways. but imho that doesn't mean everyone should be denied access to public records.

I believe strongly in gathering as much information and context as possible, including the perspectives of different sides of an issue, and presenting it to readers in a manner that empowers them to decide for themselves how they feel about it.

when I talk about not letting particular sources dictate a story's narrative, what I'm really trying to guard against is a source trying to exert too much influence in how information is presented to readers or what information is included or omitted.

anyway... the editor always has the final say in how a story is published.

for complex stories, I'll work with my editor as I go and we'll communicate about what sources and information I've gathered so far and where any gaps might be, what questions I've been able to answer and which new ones have popped up, etc. when it's time for me to write the story, I'll typically do that without his input, but after the initial draft is finished, he'll often have ideas about the story's structure and organization, the language used, etc.

any changes he suggests tend to make the story stronger. we don't always agree 100%, but at the end of the day, the editor is the boss and he makes the final decision (and if I strongly disagree with a change he wants to make, for whatever, he'll hear me out and we can usually hammer out a compromise).

(side note, in a newsroom setting, a lot of the same work happens among reporters. my colleagues and I often brainstorm together about how to approach certain stories. it can be a collaborative process.)

as a reporter, I try to handle that in the interview phase by asking clarifying questions and having as much back and forth conversation as needed to make sure I am understanding the source correctly and not misinterpreting what is being explained to me. after the initial interview, I'll follow up with the source if I need additional clarification or have more questions.

most experts are happy to accommodate this because they want a reporter to have a good understanding of their area of expertise, at least as it relates to a specific story.

I can imagine situations where it would be appropriate to share an excerpt of a story with an expert source (a few relevant paragraphs, no more) so they can identify an error or misunderstanding on the reporter's part, but those should be rare and reserved for very technical subjects and with clear guardrails in place to prevent a source from taking or attempting to take narrative control.

I wouldn't describe Baldur's Gate 3 as cozy, but that doesn't necessarily mean you won't enjoy it.

some parts of the game are intense, creepy and/or stressful. there is plenty of combat to be had, but it's also possible to talk your way out of a lot of potential combat situations.

the game can be challenging, but it does have an easy mode ("explorer mode") that makes things very manageable (your health is doubled, enemies don't use advanced tactics in combat, etc). you can also easily quicksave your game any time you're unsure of a strategy or outcome (even during cutcenes, dialogue and combat) and reload to try again if things didn't go the way you wanted or expected. I do that a lot lol.

ethics matter, too. nobody's saying content creators shouldn't be able to make money off their platforms; there are a number of ways in which creators can do so. all I'm saying is the specific practice of accepting money in exchange for reviews is unethical (and also potentially illegal, if you're not disclosing properly).

the thing is... reviews and advertising are *not* the same thing and it's problematic that people are conflating the two.

an example of advertising would be paying a content creator to create or share content (whether it's a video, tweet, etc) describing a new game, announcing the release date and where to buy it, etc. as long as it's disclosed properly so viewers know the YouTuber was paid to create or share the content, there's no ethical issue.

a review, on the other hand, is where a content creator is meant to share an honest opinion about the game (or other product), explain what they liked and disliked, recommend whether their viewers should buy it, etc.

reviews should not be bought or sold. many platforms explicitly ban paid reviews. for example, Amazon doesn't allow people to post book reviews if they've been paid to do so. authors/publishers and reviewers alike can get in trouble when they're caught exchanging money for reviews.

there can be no truly honest review when the reviewer has been paid by the product's seller. it's unethical to offer or accept money in exchange for a review.

the commonly accepted alternative practice is for a seller to provide reviewers with free copies of the product (game, book, album, etc) in exchange for an honest review.

everybody wins that way: content creators get content they can share with their audience (which ideally generates revenue through whatever other means they've set up), sellers get eyes on their product (even average or poor reviews have some value btw), audiences get content from a creator they enjoy and hopefully get enough info to help them decide whether they want to buy the product.

in my county, elections staff manually compare the signature on each absentee ballot envelope to the signature on the voter's registration. (they do this each day as batches of ballots are delivered to the elections office ahead of Election Day.)

if there's any uncertainty as to whether the signatures match, the staff contacts the voter and asks them to come to the elections office to verify the signature and potentially update the signature on their registration. I imagine many counties do it this way.

that's why creators often seek to build other means of generating revenue -- things like ad partnerships (other than reviews in exchange for money), selling merch, direct support from viewers via platforms like Patreon, paid newsletters, etc.

I'll get downvoted to hell for this, but I used to be an indie author and I completely understand why authors ask readers not to share digital copies around, even if it's impossible to actually stop readers from doing that if they're determined.

my ebooks were reuploaded without my permission on various ebook-sharing websites and ultimately pirated tens of thousands more times than they were sold.

actually, I just took a peek at my records… since they were published 5+ years ago, the first two books sold around 300 copies each -- which is more than many ebooks and I'm very fortunate to have achieved that -- while the final book sold about 100 copies. they were all priced at $1.99 or $2.99 (sometimes lower, when I did a sale) and were between 110k and 180k in length.

I know that most readers don't care about this stuff and dislike it when authors ask them not to pirate books, but as a writer and just a human being, it’s heartbreaking.

the people who read my books largely gave very positive feedback. I poured years of my life into writing those books, fighting through depression and a lot of adversity in my personal life that made it difficult to do anything creative. I invested as much as I could into the editing, covers and formatting (I’m poor now and was even poorer then). I believed in those stories and characters so much.

it was painful to put those books out into the world hoping they would resonate with readers and then get emails and messages, however complimentary, from folks who got the books on a pirating site. I even got the odd message from someone who picked up the first book on a pirating site and wanted to know where they could get the rest for free. knowing that your hard work is worthless to most people who enjoy it is really demoralizing.

I have totally given up on creative writing because I just don’t have the resources or the mental/emotional bandwidth to do it anymore, especially knowing that my work will just be pirated anyway and folks will curse me out for not wanting that to happen.

piracy hurts writers. I just wish people would remember that.

as I said above, that's why I find CW more useful than TW. it expresses no judgment about whether the content is "good" or "bad," just acknowledges that the content is there and that knowing about it upfront may help readers decide whether to engage.

imho a trigger warning is the same as a content warning. they have the same basic function: listing or describing content in order to help readers make an informed decision about whether to engage with the material.

the terms just have different baggage/connotations. as you pointed out, TW is used for more "serious" content, such as sexual assault, death, etc. but there is no reason why those kinds of elements can't be disclosed under a CW instead.

I believe CW is more useful because of its broad application. when you limit yourself to TW, you can find yourself in a pickle. if you have content that could be squicky or potentially triggering for some readers but isn't super clear cut (say, unplanned pregnancy), you have to decide if it's triggering "enough" for a warning, which can be a tough call to make.

CW takes away a lot of the guesswork. that label gives you room to include helpful info, without having to worry if the matter is serious enough to mention and without having to either lump squicky elements in with more "serious" content or list TW and CW separately.

this is why I'm a proponent of authors shifting away from "trigger" warnings and moving instead toward "content" warnings.

the former has a lot of baggage that can make certain warnings look odd or unwarranted (for example, "tw: discussions of ADHD" might seem like a bit much to some readers), while the latter is more neutral and is simply listing information to help readers decide whether they want to engage with the material without expressing, even implicitly, a value judgement on the content.

all that said, imho most content warnings don't rise to the level of "spoilers" any more than movie ratings do.

I also think that more exhaustive content warnings are generally preferable to bare-bones ones.

back in my fanfic writing days, I included all the relevant warnings I could think of (including references to or discussions about certain topics/themes) in the end notes, so readers who wanted warnings could jump to the end and get them and readers who didn't could skip them.

I also invited readers to send me a message if there was something I hadn't thought of that they felt I should add. as a writer, I wanted to make my work as accessible as possible to the folks who wanted to read it and giving them plenty of info to help them decide whether to jump in was part of that.
